Title: End Game and Rush Decks (another PTW discussion)

Messages.Author: simcof
Messages.Body:
I usually do not play rush (bruise/bleed) decks, but have started
playing them a bit now. One of the scenarios I find myself in every
now and then is that it gets towards the end, when it looks like I am
pretty close to being ousted. When it gets to my turn I have a few
freak drives etc in my hand.

If my predator has a bunch of minions, and I have rushes / freak
drives in my hand but still very low on pool (and have worked out that
I can't oust my prey this turn) my natural instinct is to rush the
hell out of my predators minions so that they can't oust me the next
turn. There has been a bit of player talk about this that this is a
real "jerk move" and not really PTW.

The rule confuses the heck out me, if I think there is a slim chance I
can still win it seems to me that I should be trying to maximize my
VPs, not just rolling over. The argument against this is that I should
just roll over because I only have a slim chance to win.

So what should I be doing in these cases if I want to play by the
tournament rules? Trying my hardest to win in a marginal situation or
rolling over?

Messages.Author: J
Messages.Body:

No, you should do whatever it takes to win.
Don't worry about what I said on JoL, I was just ribbin' you.

If you can bin enough of your predator's vamps that they can't act
against you, then you might get a round or two of grace, enough to

If you are finding it happening more and more though, then perhaps you
need to look at your deck. Maybe some more bloat/pool defence or
forward motion so that you're not just a random wrecking ball, but
have purpose on the table at all times.

-- J

If your best course of action to maximise your chances of killing your
prey is to nearly obliterate your predator, then lock'n'load.

Realistically, a moderately combat-heavy deck in a 3-play situation
should win, precisely by neutering any threatening vampire and
mangling the rest of the minions on the table. So crippling your
predator enough to buy you the time you need to do the same and then
oust your prey is as PTW as it gets. Realistically you're even
setting yourself up to claim the remaining VPs on the table (3+ VPs,
by your prey, pred, your own + VPs gained previously)

Messages.Author: J
Messages.Body:
> Realistically, a moderately combat-heavy deck in a 3-play situation
> should win

Not true.
You have to be able to deal pool damage as well, mangling a couple
vampires a turn doesn't win a game. Especially if your prey has a bit
of resistance to your fight (S:CE, Prevent or Chump Blockers), and can
deal copious pool damage. If you nuke your predator, and your prey
has some pool napalm available to them, you might have just given your
prey the GW.

-- J

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
simcof <sim...@gmail.com> wrote:
>On May 31, 11:54�am, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:

<snip - demolishing your predator when you have a slim chance to win>

>> Preventing yourself from being ousted is usually PTW.
>
>I agree, but when other players assume you have no reasonable chance
>of ousting your prey they would consider any back rushing to be just
>delaying the inevitable.

In a live tournament, delaying the inevitable is absolutely fine - if
you delay it long enough, you may push it outside the end of the round
and get a time-out .5 VP (and potentially a larger number of TP). Other
structures without the same time-out incentives won't necessarily work
like that, obviously.

An alternative may be to start on this earlier. Assuming you're
currently doing this in Turn X, if you were to start in Turn X-1 you
might get fewer people perceiving a problem, and potentially be in a
stronger position - one bleed you didn't have to deal with, one vote
etc. Obviously, not necessarily possible if you suddenly find yourself
with a new predator but...

In any event, if you see that you have a slim chance to gain VPs or win,
you can play for it. Even if other people think you're in a lost
position, you don't have to agree with them.

It may also be worth pointing out to players that this is a perfectly
rational thing for a combat deck to be doing in the late game, and that
they should plan for it. What players often mean by "You should just
roll over" is "I don't want to have to play well, so you shouldn't
expose the holes in my deck."

--
James Coupe

Again, I'm not real convinced that going backwards as a policy is a
good plan.

You sit down at a table with your rush deck. You figure out your prey.
If you can oust them quickly and brutally, you do so. In doing that,
your grand prey probably gets up to speed pretty quick and ousts their
prey. So you end up with a 3 player game pretty quickly (you with 1VP
and 6 pool; your initial grand prey/now prey with 1VP and 6 pool).
After that, you do what you need to be the last guy standing with a
3VP GW.

-Peter
